newsitem.title: INDONESIA: YEAREND-Indonesia experiences second gold rush.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Indonesia experiences second gold rush.

text.p: The glitter of gold in Indonesia has caught the eye of international mining companies, setting in train a second gold rush which mining officials expect will make the country one of the world's biggest producers.

"We are very clearly in the middle of a second gold rush in Indonesia," Paul Murphy, executive vice-president of PT Freeport Indonesia, the giant copper and gold producer in the jungles of Irian Jaya, told Reuters.

The first gold rush was in the early 1980s, involving mainly Australian companies. But only a couple out of a hundred or so explorers reached the production stage, making it "a little bit of a letdown".
There are currently five foreign companies, one state-owned company and four domestic companies exploiting gold deposits.

"Indonesia really has tremendous potential. It's a great mining frontier that is just beginning," Lou Clinton, chairman of Omax Resources Ltd, which has five projects under way in the country, said at a recent Vancouver mining conference.
BRE-X ROW OVER HUGE BUSANG GOLD FIND

Canadian exploration companies are in the forefront of the latest rush, sparked by one of the world's largest single gold finds by the small Alberta-based Bre-X Minerals Ltd in the Busang area of East Kalimantan province.
Bre-X estimates there are at least 57 million ounces of gold in the Busang field on Borneo island, currently worth over $21 billion.
But a row over ownership and development of the property has tarnished some of the glitter and caused apprehension in the mining industry over business deals in Indonesia.

The Mines and Energy Ministry pushed Bre-X into the arms of another Canadian gold company, Barrick Gold Corp. The companies say they have agreed on a 22.5-67.5 split with 10 percent going to the government.
The final details and approval have still to be announced.

Mining industry sources said such government involvement was unprecedented and could make miners wary of doing business in Indonesia -- especially as the Bre-X row also involved two members of President Suharto's family.
But mining executives and analysts are hoping the Bre-X saga is a one-off affair.
"It's an anomaly, a one-off, rather than the average," said analyst Laurie Fitgerald of Perth-based stockbroker Hartley-Poynton Ltd.
The secretary general of Mines and Energy Ministry Umar Said told Reuters Indonesia's mining policy was consistent. The Bre-X affair was an exception, he said.
SOARING GOLD PRODUCTION
Official figures show Indonesian gold production soared to over 63 tonnes in 1995 from 15.9 tonnes in 1991. The figure had reached 36.5 tonnes for the first half of 1996.
"Indonesian gold production statistics are still increasing and the exploration results are encouraging," Kuntoro Mangusubroto, director-general of mining, told Reuters.
"It is strongly believed that in the next decade Indonesia will be in fifth position among world gold producers," he said.
Kuntoro said estimated gold reserves amounted to 3,500 tonnes, excluding the huge Busang find.

He said that of the 70 sixth-generation contracts of work (COWs) awaiting presidential approval -- including two for Bre-X which are on hold -- 69 were for gold exploration. The other one was for nickel.

"Among 176 applications for seventh generation COWs, 161 applicants also intend to explore for gold, while the others are interested in nickel, copper or alluvial diamond deposits," Kuntoro said, adding that this generation would be approved in 1997.
"Gold is the prima donna," one mining executive said.

Industry sources said that traditionally about 75 percent of new finds were made by junior companies that then sold on to or teamed up with the majors who had the cash and expertise to develop the discoveries.
"With all this activity, someone is going to find something," Freeport's Murphy said.
